newsitem.title: USA: Ecuador debt boosted by poll results - US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador debt boosted by poll results - US analysts.

text.p: The popular endorsement of Ecuador interim president Fabian Alarcon in a plebiscite on Sunday bolstered political stability and buoyed Ecuador's Brady debt, U.S. analysts said.
Questions remain, however, about the referendum's impact on fiscal reform efforts in the country, they said.
Exit polls showed between 62 and 65 percent of voters endorsed Alarcon as interim president, while 74 percent of Ecuadoreans supported the February ouster of President Abdala Bucaram.
Polls conducted before the voting pegged Alarcon's support level at just above 50 percent, analysts said.

"If you can read anything into this referendum, at least it alleviates political uncertainty for the short term," said Siobhan Manning, senior Latin America analyst at Santander Investments. "(Alarcon) has never been a president on very firm footing, but at least he's not on the way out."

Ecuador Brady bonds greeted the preliminary results with a strong rally. In early afternoon trading, PDI bonds ECPDI=RR were up one percentage point at 63-5/8 bid, and Discounts ECDISC=RR were up 5/8 at 69-1/8.
But the rally would likely be short-lived, some analysts said, as the market turned its attention to fiscal measures planned for early July.

"I do expect a relief rally, but I think the tone will be much more cautious going in the July 1 public-sector price hike, because then the market will see strong signals of where we're going on the fiscal situation," Manning said.

Ecuador's 1997 budget calls for a slim 7.0-percent minimum wage increase in July, and the Alarcon administration also hopes to implement higher gasoline and cooking fuel prices at that time, Manning said.
William Romary, senior economist for Latin America at UBS Securities, said the support the referendum lends Alarcon does not add up to public support for fiscal austerity.

"A lot of people are inferring from this result that Alarcon now has a broad mandate to implement an austerity program," Romary said. "We don't think that is the case; we think he's still going to have very little room to maneuver."
Marco Santamaria, vice president in sovereign research at ING Barings, said the plebiscite promises other positive developments even if it does not immediately speed fiscal reform.
"A number of other questions ... were asked that pertain to political reform that were equally important," Santamaria said.
Among other measures, Ecuadoreans appear to have voted in favor of establishing a constituent assembly, cleaning up election finance and reforming political parties' Congressional representation.
The referendum results are based on early returns and exit polls conducted by private-sector survey firms. Official results are expected in early June.
